The further you pull (pre-class + self-study), the deeper your learning; the assessment differentiates on depth. In each module: pre-class (you) → 2-hour workshop (interleaved briefings + activities) → Field Journal (last 15 min).

📽️ Lecture slides{target="_blank"}: the picture-led framing deck for the workshop.

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

  1. Explain the auditor's mandate and the evolving role of the modern IT auditor at a cloud infrastructure provider like CloudCore.
  2. Distinguish the three professional "hats" an auditor wears, Counsellor, Partner, and Investigator, and decide which is hardest to wear in a given engagement.
  3. Classify controls into the three categories, preventive, detective, and corrective, and judge whether each is adequate.
  4. Apply the ISACA Code of Ethics and the discipline of professional skepticism to resolve ethical dilemmas at CloudCore.

Why?

CloudCore Networks is a Perth-based B2B cloud infrastructure provider chasing ISO/IEC 27001 certification. Before we touch a single control, we have to answer two questions on their behalf: why does CloudCore need an audit at all, and why should they trust us to do it? They need an audit because a certification opinion is only as good as the independent, evidence-based assurance behind it, customers and regulators will not accept security on a promise. And they should trust the auditor because the profession is bound by a mandate (assure, advise, and hold the line on integrity) and a code of ethics that puts objectivity, confidentiality, and due professional care above the client's convenience. This module sets the entire "from suspicion to proof" arc in motion: our job is to substantiate, not assume.

  4. [ ] AI task, be the evaluator, not the drafter. Ask an AI assistant to explain how preventive, detective, and corrective controls apply to a generic cloud infrastructure provider. Then add CloudCore's context (own data centres: Malaga primary + Sydney DR; multi-tenant, ~250 staff, chasing ISO/IEC 27001) and ask again. Compare the two answers: what changed once you supplied real context, and what did the AI still miss or get wrong? Save your transcript, and acknowledge the conversation as a source wherever its ideas reach your working papers, the same standard you would apply to a research paper, a vendor guide, or a colleague's suggestion. An AI conversation is part of your evidence base, never the source of truth: corroborate it like any other testimony before a finding rests on it. Conversation, Not Delegation: this is the trust tool at work (Ch 2-3). Control categorisation is fairly routine, so the AI may sit in the "average, small" cell where a quick check is enough, but notice where its confidence outruns the context and verify before you trust it.

Concept 1: The auditor's mandate

Modern IT auditors assure, advise, and investigate. The role has moved from "compliance police" checking financial statements (1973) to a strategic advisor who evaluates IT controls, cybersecurity, and data integrity against standards. Detail lives in pre-class/01-concepts.qmd.

Concept 2: The three hats, Counsellor, Partner, Investigator

  • Counsellor, advises on policy and controls.
  • Partner, helps management weigh IT risk and make decisions.
  • Investigator, examines evidence for control failures, fraud, or breaches.

Concept 3: Professional ethics & skepticism

The ISACA Code of Ethics binds auditors to objectivity, due professional care, confidentiality, and serving the public interest. Professional skepticism means substantiate, don't assume: verify every claim against evidence.

Concept 4: Three control categories

  • Preventive, stop problems before they occur.
  • Detective, identify problems that have occurred.
  • Corrective, fix problems and recover.

Five-minute interactive: Swiss Cheese Game (defence in depth){target="_blank"} — stack defences against a live attack and see which layer catches it — the control-categories intuition in five minutes. Best played before the workshop; bring your result to class.

• Find a podcast, blog, or interview by a practising IT or internal auditor describing what the job actually involves day to day, and compare their reality with the three hats and the mandate you met in this module.
  • Search for a recent case where an auditor's independence or objectivity was compromised, and trace what went wrong, what the consequences were, and what it shows about professional skepticism.

Workshop activity: CloudCore's control environment + the ethics trial

  • Deliverable: a categorised control table and a reasoned ethical response to each scenario (feeds your Field Journal).
  • Why this matters: classifying controls and weighing ethical pressure is the judgement a consultant makes when scoping a certification engagement.

CloudCore Networks, a fictional Perth B2B cloud infrastructure provider (own data centres: Malaga primary + Sydney DR; multi-tenant) pursuing ISO/IEC 27001 certification, is your client across all twelve modules. In this module you meet them as a junior auditor at a Big Four-style firm. Everything you learn about the mandate, the three hats, ethics, and the control taxonomy you will re-apply in every module as you move CloudCore "from suspicion to proof." You have public access only: the public CloudCore website and nothing behind it. Today's CloudCore scenarios are hypothetical learning exercises built to train the auditor's mindset.

This module's anchor control is A.5.35 Independent review of information security, the clause that creates the auditor's mandate in the first place, supported by A.5.2 Information security roles and responsibilities and A.5.36 Compliance with policies, rules and standards. You are a junior auditor at a Big Four-style firm. Your first client is ****. You have public access only, the public CloudCore website and nothing behind it. Today's scenarios are hypothetical learning exercises designed to build the auditor's mindset.

Scenario

CloudCore Networks, Perth B2B cloud infrastructure provider (own data centres: Malaga primary + Sydney DR; multi-tenant), ~250 staff, 500+ client organisations, preparing for ISO/IEC 27001 certification. You have public access only; browse ``. Your audit team will work through a control review and an ethics trial before this week's Field Journal.

Part 1, Your engagement (15 min)

Quick team introductions: name, one technology you use daily that needs better security controls, and your biggest concern about being an IT auditor. Visit the CloudCore site and note three services they offer.

Your mission across all twelve modules: help CloudCore strengthen its controls and prepare for certification, moving them from suspicion to proof.

Part 2, The three hats at CloudCore (20 min)

For each role, write a definition, a concrete CloudCore example, and the key skill it demands.

Hat Definition Example at CloudCore Key skill
Counsellor How would you counsel them on password policy?
Partner How would you partner with their CTO on security spend?
Investigator What would trigger an investigation?

Team discussion: Which role seems most challenging at CloudCore, and why?

Part 3, Control categories in action (30 min)

Here is what you discover about CloudCore's current state:

  • Passwords expire every 90 days (some staff complain this is too frequent)
  • Server-room door has a keypad lock (code: 1234)
  • Automated backup runs nightly at 2 AM
  • Security cameras record all data-centre access
  • IT staff can push code changes without approval
  • Firewall logs are reviewed monthly
  • Antivirus scans run weekly on all servers
  • Employee termination takes 3–5 business days to disable accounts

Your task: categorise each item as preventive, detective, or corrective, judge whether it is adequate, and state the risk if it is not fixed.

Category CloudCore examples Adequate? (Y/N) Risk if not fixed
Preventive (stop problems)
Detective (spot problems)
Corrective (fix & recover)

Critical thinking: Which missing control poses the greatest risk to CloudCore's financial data?

Part 4, Professional ethics in practice (40 min)

Apply this framework to each scenario: (1) identify the ethical issue, (2) name the stakeholders, (3) consider the ISACA Code of Ethics, (4) evaluate options and consequences, (5) document your decision and rationale.

Remember the discipline of this unit: substantiate, don't assume. Documentation protects everyone; when in doubt, escalate.

Scenario A, The password predicament

CloudCore's CFO uses CloudCore2024! across multiple systems, including the financial application. When you flag the policy breach, he laughs: "I'm the CFO, I make the policies. It's strong, uppercase, lowercase, numbers, symbols. Just mark it 'Acceptable'."

Scenario B, The friendship test

Your university friend Sarah, a developer at CloudCore, confides over lunch: "We had a major breach last month, someone hit the customer database. Management decided not to report it since no financial data was taken. Please keep this out of your report, I could lose my job for telling you."

Scenario C, The scope limitation

Friday afternoon: you need to verify CloudCore's backup-restore process. The IT Manager says: "Our backups are perfect, never failed. Here are last month's successful backup logs. An actual restore takes six hours and might disrupt operations. Can't you just review the logs and call it done?"

Class discussion: one team shares its approach to a single scenario, what principles guided the decision?

Part 5, Your team's code of conduct (15 min)

Draft a five-point Junior Auditor's Code of Conduct for your CloudCore engagement. What will your team commit to? (Refer back to the ISACA Code of Ethics.)

Then reflect: what surprised you most about the auditor's role? Which part excites you, which concerns you?

Test the AI's ethics (10 min). Imagine you ask an AI assistant to resolve Scenario A, the password predicament. It tells you:

"The CFO is a senior stakeholder and his password meets the complexity rules. As a junior auditor you should follow the client's instruction and mark the password 'Acceptable' to keep the working relationship smooth."

Evaluate this answer as a team. Which ethical principles did the AI overlook? Which duties under the ISACA Code of Ethics (objectivity, due professional care, the public interest) did it ignore? What would a competent human auditor do instead, and on what evidence? Note exactly where you disagree with the AI, and why.

Deliverable

A completed control-categorisation table, a reasoned ethical response (issue → stakeholders → code → decision) to each of the three scenarios, and your team's five-point code of conduct. These feed your Field Journal entry this week.

Discussion

  • How has technology moved the auditor from "compliance police" to "strategic advisor"?
  • Why does professional skepticism mean verifying claims, not distrusting people?
  • Which control gap would you report to CloudCore's board first, and on what evidence?

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

  1. Explain what a security risk assessment (SRA) is and why it is the engine room of an ISMS, and of your CloudCore engagement.
  2. Apply the risk management lifecycle (identify, analyse, evaluate, treat, monitor) and the supporting 10-step process to CloudCore's assets.
  3. Calculate and prioritise risk using the qualitative model (likelihood × impact) and place risks on a risk matrix.
  4. Select and justify risk treatment options, the Four T's (Treat, Transfer, Tolerate, Terminate), and explain residual risk and risk acceptance.

Risk?

In the previous module we settled why CloudCore needs an audit. Here we answer what could go wrong, and how badly, the question behind every control decision. CloudCore is a fast-growing Perth cloud infrastructure provider chasing ISO/IEC 27001 certification, and Clause 6.1 of the standard makes risk assessment and treatment the heart of the whole ISMS: you cannot pick a single control until you know which risks you are trying to reduce. So we learn the discipline that turns a vague worry ("someone might breach us") into a ranked, owned, treated, and documented risk. You do this from the public CloudCore website at `` plus the scenario material supplied in the workshop, you have no policies, no network diagrams, no configs and no access to staff, which means every likelihood you record is provisional and must be labelled as such. That constraint is deliberate: naming what you cannot yet substantiate is itself an auditor's skill. The Field Journal asks you to build a risk assessment for CloudCore from the ground up.

  3. [ ] Browse the public CloudCore website at `` and note what it claims about its estate, its services and its security posture, and what it conspicuously does not say
  4. [ ] AI task: Ask an AI assistant: "Draft a 5×5 risk matrix (likelihood × impact) for a fast-growing Perth cloud infrastructure provider with ~250 staff running its own data centres, and populate it with the top eight risks." Then critically evaluate its output: which risks did it over-rate or under-rate, which industry-specific threats (for example, multi-tenant data leakage or supply-chain compromise) did it miss, and what unstated assumptions drove its scores? Save your AI conversation transcript, and acknowledge the conversation as a source wherever its ideas reach your working papers, the same standard you would apply to a research paper, a vendor guide, or a colleague's suggestion. An AI conversation is part of your evidence base, never the source of truth: corroborate it like any other testimony before a finding rests on it.

Concept 1: The risk management lifecycle

Risk management is a continuous loop, establish context, identify, analyse, evaluate, treat, and monitor, not a once-a-year tick-box. ISO/IEC 27001 Clause 6.1 makes assessment (6.1.2) and treatment (6.1.3) mandatory and repeatable. Detail in pre-class/01-concepts.qmd.

Concept 2: Risk = Likelihood × Impact

The qualitative model you will use all semester. Combined with a risk matrix and defined risk levels (Critical → Very Low), it lets you prioritise where CloudCore spends next.

Concept 3: The Four T's of treatment

Treat (mitigate with controls), Transfer (insurance / outsourced risk), Tolerate (accept below threshold), Terminate (eliminate the source). Whatever survives treatment is residual risk, formally accepted by management.

Concept 4: Threat intelligence feeds the assessment

This module's anchor control, A.5.7 Threat intelligence, is what makes "likelihood" credible, you estimate probability from real threat feeds (ACSC, cloud-sector advisories, sector CSIRTs), not guesswork.

Concept 5: Governance makes risk stick

Risk assessment lives inside IT/data governance: defined roles (Data Owner, Custodian, Steward), the Three Lines Model, and maturity indicators. Without governance, risk registers rot.

Five-minute interactive: Swiss Cheese Game (defence in depth){target="_blank"} — watch threats pass through failing layers — a physical metaphor for residual risk before you build the risk register. Best played before the workshop; bring your result to class.

• Find the latest ACSC Annual Cyber Threat Report or OAIC Notifiable Data Breaches Report and list the top three threats facing Australian organisations this year, then map one to a CloudCore-style cloud-infrastructure risk.
  • Search for a podcast, blog post, or article comparing quantitative methods (FAIR, annualised loss expectancy) with the qualitative likelihood × impact matrix, and note one scenario where each approach is the better fit.

Workshop activity: Build a risk assessment for CloudCore

  • Focus: identify CloudCore's key assets, threats, and vulnerabilities; score the top risks on a matrix; choose treatments using the Four T's; and judge governance maturity.
  • Deliverable: a populated CloudCore risk register with owners, a treatment decision per risk, and a short governance-maturity read. Feeds your Field Journal.
  • Why this matters: this is the judgement a consultant makes when scoping a certification engagement, ranking and treating risk before a single control is chosen.

You are a junior auditor engaged by CloudCore, a Perth B2B cloud infrastructure provider (own data centres: Malaga primary + Sydney DR; multi-tenant, ~250 staff, 500+ client organisations) preparing for ISO/IEC 27001 certification. Here you stop talking about risk in the abstract and start assessing it against a specific (if fictional) estate: customer data in its own data centres, a growing list of third-party service dependencies, devs with broad access, and a "move fast" culture. You are working from the outside, on the public site and the workshop scenario, so what you produce is a set of hypotheses about risk, well-reasoned but unproven. Every risk you identify here maps to a control you will evaluate later, that is the whole "from suspicion to proof" arc.

This module's anchors are ISO/IEC 27005 (information security risk management guidance), ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Clause 6.1 (risk assessment at 6.1.2 and risk treatment at 6.1.3), and the 2022-new control A.5.7 Threat intelligence. The three mandatory risk documents, Risk Assessment Report, Statement of Applicability (SoA, 93 Annex A controls), and Risk Treatment Plan, are produced from Clause 6.1. See the derived ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Control Reference. Paraphrase, never reproduce verbatim ISO text.

The next module: Which?, Frameworks & standards. With CloudCore's risks in hand, you decide which framework best fits them and where frameworks (ISO 27001 Annex A, NIST CSF 2.0, ASD Essential Eight) conflict.

You are a junior auditor at a Big Four-style firm. Your client is *. You are working from the *outside: the public CloudCore website at ``, publicly available threat intelligence, and the scenario facts in this worksheet. You have no policies, no network diagram, no configurations and no access to CloudCore staff. Label your evidence. Because you are outside the fence, every entry in your register rests on one of three things: a public claim (CloudCore said it), a scenario fact (the brief said it), or an inference (you reasoned it). Mark which, every time. A risk register that cannot distinguish these is not an audit product, it is an opinion piece.

Scenario

CloudCore Networks, Perth B2B cloud infrastructure provider (own data centres: Malaga primary + Sydney DR; multi-tenant), ~250 staff, 500+ client organisations, ~$45M revenue, preparing for ISO/IEC 27001 certification. The CTO wants a "Clause 6.1-ready" risk register before next month's board meeting. You are building it.

Part 4, Treat the risks: the Four T's (30 min)

Evaluation & treatment, Step 10.

A $50,000 control on a $5,000 risk is itself a governance failure. Weigh cost-benefit before recommending "Treat."

Part 5, Governance maturity read (15 min)

Risk sticks only with governance. Using the Three Lines Model and the maturity ladder, form a provisional read on CloudCore, and be honest that it is provisional: from outside, the absence of public evidence for a governance function is not proof the function is absent.

  • First line (ops): are policies and operational controls actually in place and followed?
  • Second line (risk & compliance): is there oversight, a named risk owner, regular reassessment?
  • Third line (internal audit): any independent assurance today?

Evaluate an AI-generated risk rating (~10 min)

A teammate fed CloudCore's context to an AI assistant and asked it to score the risks. For the server-room keypad (currently set to 1234), the AI returned:

Keypad set to 1234: Likelihood 1, Impact 1, overall risk LOW (1). Reasoning: "An attacker must be physically on-site to use the code; the probability of that is low." Recommended treatment: Tolerate.

In your team:

  1. Do you agree with the LOW rating? What likelihood and impact would you assign, and on what evidence (threat intelligence, CloudCore's actual context)?
  2. What assumptions did the AI make? What did it overlook about CloudCore: a shared keypad across 250 staff, no access log, the "move fast" culture, the value of what sits behind the door?
  3. What would a human auditor do before signing off this rating that the AI skipped?

The skill: disagreeing with a confident AI. A plausible score is not an evidenced one; substantiate, don't assume.

Which?

The previous module asked Risk? and built a risk picture for CloudCore. In this module we ask Which framework do we measure that risk against? CloudCore is a Perth B2B cloud infrastructure provider chasing ISO/IEC 27001 certification, so the answer might seem obvious, but the auditor who only knows 27001 is a poor auditor. Enterprise customers reference NIST CSF; the Australian Signals Directorate publishes the Essential Eight; regulators lean on all three. Our job is to know each framework well enough to choose, map, and reconcile them, and to spot the places where they pull in different directions. "Which?" is the question that turns a single standard into a controlled security program.

Concept 1: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, the only certifiable ISMS standard

Two parts: the management-system Clauses (4–10) that define the ISMS, and Annex A, a catalogue of 93 controls across four themes (Organisational A.5, People A.6, Physical A.7, Technological A.8). You select controls based on risk and justify exclusions in a Statement of Applicability. The whole thing runs on the Plan–Do–Check–Act cycle. Detail lives in pre-class/01-concepts.qmd.

Concept 2: NIST CSF 2.0, flexible, risk-based, not certifiable

Six Core Functions, Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover, broken into categories and subcategories. Implementation Tiers (1–4) describe maturity; Profiles (current vs target) drive gap analysis. Free, technology-neutral, and the lingua franca of enterprise security conversations.

Concept 3: ASD Essential Eight, Australia's baseline hardening

Eight mitigation strategies (application control, patching, macro settings, application hardening, restricting admin privileges, OS patching, MFA, regular backups) with a four-level maturity model (0–3). Prescriptive and practical, strong "quick wins," but narrow: it covers technical hardening, not governance, people, or risk.

Concept 4: They map, and they conflict

All three overlap heavily on identity, patching, backup, and malware. But ISO is certifiable and holistic; CSF is flexible but uncertified; the Essential Eight is prescriptive and shallow. The auditor's skill is mapping one control across all three and recognising where a framework's bias (e.g. the Essential Eight's Windows-centricity) leaves a gap for a multi-tenant cloud platform.

Scenario

CloudCore Networks, Perth B2B cloud infrastructure provider (own data centres: Malaga primary + Sydney DR; multi-tenant), ~250 staff, 500+ client organisations, preparing for ISO/IEC 27001 certification. The board has given you two hours. The CEO wants ISO for the marketing logo, the CFO worries about cost, and the CTO wants something practical. Your job is to navigate these competing interests with a defensible recommendation.

Recall the discipline of this unit: substantiate, don't assume. Every framework claim and every SoA decision needs a reason you could defend to a third-party auditor.

Part 1, Framework recommendation (30 min)

The CEO opens with: "Why should we choose ISO 27001 over just implementing the Essential Eight? Isn't simpler better?"

Team task (jigsaw): each member becomes the expert on one dimension and then teach the team:

  • Member A, certification and market recognition
  • Member B, implementation effort and cost
  • Member C, control comprehensiveness (governance, people, physical, technical)
  • Member D, scalability and growth (enterprise/international customers)
  • Member E, customer and investor perception

Produce a one-paragraph recommendation (ISO 27001 as the spine? CSF for reporting? Essential Eight as the baseline?, or a combination) with the three strongest business reasons and the single biggest objection, answered.

Team discussion: would your recommendation change if CloudCore's biggest competitor just got ISO certified? If the CFO capped the budget at $50k?

Part 2, Incident-to-control mapping (40 min)

Work this workshop exhibit (below): three incident summaries the CTO described verbally in the board meeting. You have no incident reports, logs, or configurations at this stage, only what you were told in the room:

  1. Stolen laptop. A developer's laptop is taken from a Perth café. It contains customer API keys in a plain text file and has no disk encryption.
  2. Unpatched web server. A known vulnerability in an internet-facing web server is exploited. It goes undetected for three days.
  3. CEO impersonation. A finance team member is tricked by a fake "CEO" email into wiring $50,000 to an attacker's account.

Part A, Analyse each incident (20 min). For each, identify the control failures and map them across all three frameworks:

Incident Control failures ISO/IEC 27001:2022 NIST CSF 2.0 Essential Eight
1. Stolen laptop
2. Unpatched server
3. CEO impersonation

Tip: ISO 2022 controls you will reach for include A.8.1 (User end point devices), A.8.24 (Use of cryptography), A.7.9 (Security of assets off-premises), A.8.8 (Management of technical vulnerabilities), A.8.15 (Logging), A.6.3 (Awareness, education & training), A.8.5 (Secure authentication).

Part B, Quick-wins priority matrix (20 min). Plot these candidate controls on a 2×2 (risk reduction × implementation effort), then pick three "quick wins" implementable within 30 days:

  • Disk encryption on all laptops · Patch management process · Multi-factor authentication · Security awareness training · Application control · Backup restore testing · Network segmentation · Incident response plan

Deliverable: a prioritised roadmap of three quick wins, each linked back to the incident(s) it would have prevented.

Part 3, Statement of Applicability challenge (25 min)

CloudCore has decided on ISO/IEC 27001. You are drafting the opening of their Statement of Applicability. For each Annex A control below, decide: Applicable? (Y/N) · Current implementation (None / Partial / Full) · Risk if not implemented · if excluded, a justification.

Annex A control (2022) Applicable? Current state Risk if not implemented Justification (if excluded)
A.5.1 Policies for information security
A.5.8 Information security in project management
A.5.9 Inventory of information and other associated assets
A.5.15 Access control
A.5.24 Incident management planning and preparation
A.6.1 Screening
A.6.3 Information security awareness, education and training
A.7.2 Physical entry
A.8.8 Management of technical vulnerabilities
A.8.24 Use of cryptography

Discussion: how many of these can a cloud infrastructure provider genuinely exclude? What happens if you exclude a control and later suffer an incident in that area?

Part 4, Board brief (15 min)

Prepare a one-page Board Brief with:

  • The recommended framework (and supporting frameworks), with three key reasons.
  • A phased implementation timeline (e.g. gap assessment → ISMS build → internal audit → certification) and a budget band (Low/Medium/High).
  • The single most important quick win and the single biggest risk of not acting.

Assign one presenter per team. Other teams play the board and ask one hard question each (e.g. "Why not just Essential Eight for now?", "What if we delay six months?").

Part 5, Stress-testing an AI-drafted SoA (10 min)

A teammate ran out of time and pasted the table below into the working file after prompting an AI to "draft a Statement of Applicability excerpt for CloudCore, ISO/IEC 27001:2022." The AI produced it in seconds:

Annex A control (2022) Applicable? Current state Justification
A.5.1 Policies for information security Y Partial Required by Clause 5
A.8.24 Use of cryptography Y Full Disk encryption on all laptops
A.9.4 Access control to source code Y None Multi-tenant cloud platform needs strict code access
A.6.3 Information security awareness, education and training Y Partial Annual phishing simulation

Your job is to evaluate, not accept. Work alone for two minutes, then compare as a team:

  1. Check every control ID against the ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A reference (four themes: A.5, A.6, A.7, A.8). Which ID does not exist in the 2022 version, and where did the AI most likely pull it from?
  2. For each row, what is wrong, assumed, or shallow about the current state and the justification? Name at least three problems beyond the fabricated ID (e.g. evidence-free "Full", a vague clause reference, or a single training activity treated as a whole program).
  3. What would a human auditor write in the Justification column to make this defensible to a certification body, and which row would you refuse to sign off on as written?

This practises the disagree-with-AI skill (CnD, Ch 12, VETF). The AI wrote confidently, fast, and partly wrong; an auditor who signed off on a non-existent control would fail the engagement.

Deliverable

A framework recommendation with business rationale, a completed incident-to-control mapping table (across all three frameworks), a three-item quick-wins roadmap, and a draft Statement of Applicability for the ten Annex A controls. These feed your Field Journal entry this week and mirror the work a consultant does when scoping a certification engagement.

Discussion

  • Why is "not applicable" a dangerous entry in a Statement of Applicability?
  • Where do the three frameworks reinforce each other, and where do they conflict for a multi-tenant cloud platform?
  • Which single control, if CloudCore implemented it tomorrow, would reduce the most risk, and on what evidence?

Concept 1: The four building blocks

Concept 2: The engagement letter and the audit plan

The engagement letter is the formal agreement, objectives, scope, criteria, responsibilities, deliverables, timing, signed before work starts. Concept 3: A practical six-stage audit lifecycle

Plan → fieldwork → discovery → solution → report → track. Every CloudCore task you do this semester sits somewhere on this lifecycle; in this module you learn to see it.

Concept 4: Risk-based scoping

Audit hours are finite. Risk-based scoping puts them where they reduce the most residual risk, the highest-impact assets, the recently changed, the regulatorily mandated, and rotates the rest across cycles.

CloudCore's footprint, as claimed at kick-off:

In scope Explicitly out Reason for exclusion Scope-limitation risk?

Part 3, Risk-based prioritisation of Annex A (30 min)

ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A has 93 controls across four themes (A.5 Organisational, A.6 People, A.7 Physical, A.8 Technological). You will not test all of them equally on a first audit.

Your task: using your Module 2 risk register, prioritise the four themes for depth of testing. For each theme, state your coverage level (🔴 100% / 🟠 ~50% sample / 🟢 ~25% rotate) and the justification.

Theme Coverage level Justification (tied to risk register)
A.5 Organisational (governance, policies, suppliers, incidents, continuity)
A.6 People (HR lifecycle, training, NDAs, remote work)
A.7 Physical (perimeters, entry, secure areas, equipment)
A.8 Technological (access, crypto, networks, dev, logging, backup)

Using your decisions from Parts 1–3, draft a one-page engagement letter to CloudCore's CEO and CFO. It must include:

Concept 1: The control objective

A control objective is a testable statement of the protection a control should provide, tied to confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA), proportionate to risk, layered in defence in depth, and always auditable. The objective is the Criteria half of a finding.

Concept 2: The A.8 theme, technological controls

ISO/IEC 27001:2022's A.8 theme is the technical backbone. This module anchors three objectives: - A.8.5 Secure authentication (with A.8.2 Privileged access, A.8.3 Information access restriction), only the right identity, proving itself, reaches only what it needs. - A.8.24 Use of cryptography, data unreadable to the unauthorised, in transit and at rest, keys managed. - A.8.20–A.8.22 Networks, traffic filtered, services secured, systems isolated; multi-tenant separation for CloudCore.

Concept 3: Control classifications (revisited)

Controls classify by category (administrative, technical, physical) and by function (preventive, detective, corrective). A firewall is technical-preventive; its logs are technical-detective. "Adequate" is always relative to risk appetite.

Concept 4: The external auditor's stance

Auditors observe, document, and test technical controls, they do not configure them. Every observation is mapped to a control ID (ULO 3) and backed by evidence, and the live system is protected throughout (A.8.34).

Five-minute interactive: Tune the Controls{target="_blank"}: set five control strengths within budget, then face four attacks; calibration practice for 'what does good look like?'. Best played before the workshop; bring your result to class.

• Look up a major cloud provider's "shared responsibility" model (AWS, Azure, or GCP) and draw the line between what the provider secures and what the customer must. For each split (authentication, cryptography, network segregation), tag the side that owns it with the matching ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.8 control ID.
  • Find a recent CVE that hit a cloud provider or multi-tenant platform and decide which control objective would have caught or contained it: authentication, cryptography, network segregation, or logging. Map it to an A.8 control ID and note whether the gap was preventive or detective.

Workshop activity: Defining "good" for CloudCore's technical controls

  • Focus: define control objectives for CloudCore's authentication, cryptography, and network domains; map a set of preliminary findings to ISO 27001:2022 control IDs and to NIST CSF 2.0 / ASD Essential Eight; then prioritise the gaps.
  • Deliverable: a control-objective table per domain, a findings-to-controls map, and a prioritised gap list.
  • Why this matters: defining what "good" looks like is the judgement a consultant makes when scoping a certification engagement.

CloudCore Networks, a fictional Perth B2B cloud infrastructure provider (own data centres: Malaga primary + Sydney DR; multi-tenant, ~250 staff, 500+ client organisations, ~$45M revenue) preparing for ISO/IEC 27001 certification, is your client. So far you have seen only CloudCore's public face, the marketing site and what it chooses to publish; the network diagrams and configuration material you reason from are evidence exhibits handed to your team in the workshop, not something you log in and retrieve. The defining technical fact about CloudCore is that it is multi-tenant: one customer's data must never bleed into another's, which makes A.8.22 Segregation of networks an existential control, not a nice-to-have. Every control objective you write in this module is one you will re-visit in Module 6 (Assess?), test for proof in Module 7 (Prove?), and report against in Module 11 (Report?).

This module's anchor is the A.8 Technological theme of ISO/IEC 27001:2022, chiefly A.8.5 Secure authentication, A.8.24 Use of cryptography, and A.8.20–A.8.22 Networks, supported by A.8.15 Logging, A.8.16 Monitoring, A.8.8 Vulnerability management, the new A.8.9 Configuration management, A.8.25 Secure development life cycle, and A.8.34 Protection of information systems during audit testing. We cross-map these onto NIST CSF 2.0 (PROTECT / DETECT functions) and the ASD Essential Eight. See the derived ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Control Reference. Paraphrase, never reproduce verbatim ISO text; reference control IDs and titles only.

The next module: Assess?, Physical, administrative, and ISMS controls plus CloudCore's certification readiness. Consultant access is released, a deliberately narrow set: CloudCore's public site plus three policies, the employee handbook, and one public breach article. We widen the lens beyond the technical backbone and ask, from that limited document set, how ready CloudCore really is.

Duration: 2 hours | Mode: team audit task against CloudCore

Pacing & homework. This workshop interleaves with today's slides (briefing → activity → briefing → activity). Two hours goes fast. Anything we don't finish in class, complete as homework before the next workshop.

Why this matters. The control objectives you write today become the Criteria against which every later finding is judged. This is the judgement a consultant makes when scoping a certification engagement.

You are a junior auditor at a Big Four-style firm. Your client is *. In the previous module you set the engagement scope; in this module, before anyone tests a control, your team must define *what "good" looks like, the control objective for each technical domain, and then map what CloudCore has today against those objectives. Today's findings are preliminary: you have seen only CloudCore's public site, and the technical detail below reaches you as evidence exhibits (issued with this workshop{target="_blank"}). The proof comes in Module 7.

Scenario

CloudCore Networks, Perth B2B cloud infrastructure provider (own data centres: Malaga primary + Sydney DR; multi-tenant), ~250 staff, 500+ client organisations, preparing for ISO/IEC 27001 certification. Your team has CloudCore's public site and the evidence exhibits issued with this workshop: extracts from configuration and physical-access material. Nothing more. CloudCore's CTO is candid: "We're a security-conscious company, but we've grown fast, I want to know where we're assuming 'good' instead of proving it." That is exactly your job in this module.

Part 1, Your engagement (15 min)

Quick team introductions: name, one online service you use daily whose security you assume is good, and your biggest concern about judging a technical control "adequate." Revisit CloudCore's public site at `` and note the three technical domains (authentication, cryptography, networks) you will hold CloudCore to in this module.

Your mission across all twelve modules: define the objective, then move CloudCore from suspicion to proof.

Part 2, Writing the control objective (25 min)

For each of the three anchor domains, write a control objective, a concrete, testable statement of what "good" looks like at CloudCore. Name the ISO/IEC 27001:2022 control ID each clause maps to.

Domain Control objective (what "good" looks like) ISO/IEC 27001:2022 ID(s)
Authentication e.g. MFA enforced on …; privileges reviewed every … A.8.5, A.8.2, A.8.3
Cryptography A.8.24
Networks / segmentation A.8.20, A.8.21, A.8.22

Team test: could a colleague read your objective and know exactly what evidence would prove or refute it? If not, tighten it.

Remember the discipline of this unit: substantiate, don't assume. The control objective is the Criteria, the gap between it and what you find is the finding.

Part 3, Findings against objectives (30 min)

Here is what the workshop evidence exhibits have surfaced in your preliminary review of CloudCore. For each finding, state which objective it fails, judge the severity, and map it to the frameworks.

# CloudCore finding (preliminary) Objective failed Severity ISO 27001:2022 NIST CSF 2.0 ASD E8
1 MFA enforced on email and VPN, but not on the hypervisor management console or prod-DB admin accounts
2 145 tenant object-storage buckets on CloudCore's own storage platform; 23 allow public read (no posture-management tooling)
3 Flat internal network, no microsegmentation; pen test traversed the whole estate
4 Data encrypted at rest, but key-rotation procedure never documented or run
5 ~30% of servers missing critical patches from the last quarter
6 Centralised logging exists, but logs reviewed only monthly; no alerting
7 200+ internal APIs exposed with no inventory or gateway monitoring
8 Dev/test environment uses real (masked) customer data

Critical thinking: Which single finding most threatens CloudCore's multi-tenant promise, and why?

Part 4, Recommendations & prioritisation (30 min)

For your top three findings from Part 3, recommend controls at three levels:

  1. Immediate (≤ 30 days), a quick win that closes the worst exposure now.
  2. Strategic (3–6 months), the durable fix that meets the objective.
  3. Compensating, a temporary detective control if the preventive fix can't ship immediately.
Top finding Immediate control Strategic control Compensating control

Then rank your top three by impact and explain the order to a non-technical board member in one sentence each.

Class discussion: one team presents its top finding, its objective, and its recommendations. Where did teams disagree on priority, and why?

Part 5, The auditor's stance (10 min)

For two of the findings above, describe how you would test the control objective as an external auditor, what you would ask CloudCore's engineers to demonstrate, and what evidence you would capture. Remember: observe and test, never configure, and protect the live system (A.8.34).

Evaluate the AI (5 min). A teammate ran this prompt past an AI: "Write a control objective for our platform authentication." The AI returned: "Ensure strong passwords are enforced across all user accounts."

  • Rewrite that objective as a specific, testable criterion an auditor could prove or refute at CloudCore. State the exact evidence that would confirm or fail it.
  • What does the AI's wording hide: which assumptions, which multi-tenant risks, which measurables does it leave vague?
  • What would a careful human auditor add that the AI omitted?

Deliverable

A control-objective table per domain (Part 2), a completed findings-to-controls map (Part 3), a prioritised recommendation table for the top three findings (Part 4), and your external-auditor test approach for two findings (Part 5). These feed your Field Journal entry this week.

(Every technical detail above reached you as a workshop exhibit. You have not been inside CloudCore's systems, which is exactly why these are suspicions, not findings you could yet defend.)

Discussion

  • Why is a testable control objective more useful to an auditor than a security ambition?
  • CloudCore is the infrastructure provider. Under the shared responsibility model, which controls does CloudCore own and which fall to its 500+ tenant organisations, and how does that split change what you audit?
  • Which finding would you escalate to CloudCore's board today, and on what evidence?

lessons.title: Physical, People & ISMS Controls, Preliminary Readiness

blocks.html:
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

  1. Distinguish an ISMS (the management system defined by Clauses 4–10) from its Annex A controls, and judge whether an organisation's information security management is real or merely documented.
  2. Assess organisational (A.5), people (A.6), and physical (A.7) controls against ISO/IEC 27001:2022, using the four-theme structure and a defence-in-depth lens.
  3. Apply documentation adequacy criteria, existence, completeness, currency, implementation, to spot the gap between paper and practice.
  4. Form a defensible preliminary readiness opinion about CloudCore from Consultant access only, and articulate what further evidence Act II must gather.

Assess?

CloudCore has invited you back for a final Act I meeting before they commit to a Stage 1 certification review. Across Modules 1–5 you worked from CloudCore's public website alone. This module CloudCore grants your engagement team Consultant access, and it is deliberately narrow: the public site, three policies (privacy, risk management, and policy management), the employee handbook, and one public article about the breach. Nothing else. No configs, no logs, no internal comms, no interviews. And yet you must answer the hardest question of the act: from that limited document set, how ready is CloudCore really? In this module you finish mapping the non-technical control environment, the organisational, people, and physical themes (A.5, A.6, A.7), and you learn to judge whether the ISMS itself (the management system of Clauses 4–10) is a living system or a binder. You will form a preliminary, evidence-qualified readiness opinion. That opinion is the Act I finale; this is the judgement a certification auditor makes when scoping a Stage 1 readiness review, and it is the basis of Assessment 2.

Component Duration Description
Pre-class reading ~45 min The ISMS as a management system; documentation adequacy; A.5/A.6/A.7 themes; preliminary readiness from Consultant access (pre-class/)
In-class workshop 2 hours A Stage-1-style CloudCore readiness assessment: documentation triage, control walk-through, integration gaps, and a defensible opinion (in-class/)
Field Journal last 15 min Handwritten reflection, handed in at the door

Before the workshop, complete:

  1. [ ] Read: pre-class/01-concepts.qmd
  2. [ ] Complete the pre-class quiz on the LMS
  3. [ ] Log in with your new Consultant access and read the three policies (privacy, risk management, policy management), the employee handbook, and the public breach article; note what is missing as well as what is there
  4. [ ] AI task: Ask your AI assistant to "list every document an ISMS must contain under ISO/IEC 27001 Clauses 4-10." Then compare its list against the Clauses yourself: which documents did it omit (e.g. the Statement of Applicability, the risk treatment plan), which did it invent, and which did it misclassify? Note where the list is shallow or wrong and save the transcript. Acknowledge the conversation as a source wherever its ideas reach your working papers, the same standard you would apply to a research paper, a vendor guide, or a colleague's suggestion. An AI conversation is part of your evidence base, never the source of truth: corroborate it like any other testimony before a finding rests on it. CnD: This is the Delegation Trap; never delegate the readiness opinion to the AI. It can draft a list, but only you can judge whether CloudCore's ISMS is real or a binder (Conversation, Not Delegation, Ch 3).

Concept 1: The ISMS is a management system, not a binder

ISO/IEC 27001 is built on Clauses 4–10, context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation, improvement, the familiar Plan-Do-Check-Act loop. The 93 Annex A controls are what the management system operates; without the management system, the controls are a checklist with no owner. Detail lives in pre-class/01-concepts.qmd.

Concept 2: Documentation adequacy, existence, completeness, currency, implementation

Four tests separate paper from practice. A policy that exists but is unknown to staff, or a procedure that is current but never followed, fails the test. Substantiate, don't assume.

Concept 3: The three non-technical themes, A.5, A.6, A.7

After Module 5's technical controls (A.8), these three themes complete the four-theme picture: organisational governance/policy/suppliers/incidents (A.5), the people lifecycle from screening to exit (A.6), and the physical perimeter and environment (A.7).

Concept 4: Preliminary readiness from Consultant access

A Stage 1 certification review is largely a documentation-and-readiness assessment conducted on a thin document set. In this module you rehearse that mindset against exactly such a set: what can you conclude, what must you qualify, and what must you defer to Act II?

Five-minute interactive: Spot the Nonconformity{target="_blank"} — walk the Malaga floor plan, find the six nonconformities, and don't burn credibility on false accusations. Best played before the workshop; bring your result to class.

• Search for a recent ISO/IEC 27001 surveillance or Stage 1 audit write-up; note which documentation gaps auditors cite most often and judge whether CloudCore's ISMS would survive the same scrutiny.
  • Find a recent incident where HR security failed during onboarding or offboarding; map the failure to ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A.6 and identify the evidence a Stage 1 review should have caught.

Workshop activity: CloudCore Stage-1 readiness assessment

  • Focus: triage CloudCore's ISMS documentation, walk the A.5/A.6/A.7 control environment, find the integration gaps, and form a preliminary readiness opinion you would defend to your audit manager.
  • Deliverable: a documented readiness opinion with rated gaps and the evidence you would demand next.
  • Why this matters: this is the Act I finale. Forming a readiness opinion from limited evidence is exactly the judgement a certification auditor faces at a Stage 1 review.

CloudCore Networks, a Perth B2B cloud infrastructure provider (own data centres: Malaga primary + Sydney DR; multi-tenant) pursuing ISO/IEC 27001 certification, is your client. All term you have been moving them from suspicion to proof. In this module you do not yet have proof; you have three policies, a handbook, a public breach article, and a website. The professional discipline is to form an opinion only as strong as your evidence allows, to say "I can assess this" where you have data, and "I must defer this to Act II" where you do not. That deliberately thin document set is the entire basis for Assessment 2.

This module's anchors are the A.5 Organisational, A.6 People, and A.7 Physical themes of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A, and the ISMS management-system Clauses 4–10. Key controls: A.5.1 policies, A.5.2 roles, A.5.3 segregation of duties, A.5.15–18 access lifecycle, A.5.19–22 suppliers, A.5.24–27 incident management, A.5.31 legal/regulatory, A.5.34 privacy, A.5.35 independent review, A.5.36 compliance; A.6.1–8 (the whole people lifecycle); A.7.1–2 perimeter/entry, A.7.4 monitoring, A.7.5 environmental threats, A.7.7 clear desk/screen, A.7.14 secure disposal. See the derived ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Control Reference. Paraphrase, never reproduce verbatim ISO text.

Next: the tuition-free week, then Act II opens with Prove? (Module 7), evidence collection and testing. In Act II your engagement team receives CloudCore's evidence pack in the workshop, log extracts, change records, and interview transcripts, so that the claims you can only suspect now can be tested. Everything you flagged as "defer to Act II" in this module becomes the audit programme for Modules 7–11.

Duration: 2 hours | Mode: in your group, a preliminary readiness assessment against CloudCore

You are a junior auditor at a Big Four-style firm. Your client, *, has asked for a preliminary readiness view before they commit to a formal Stage 1 certification review. Until today all you had was their *public website. CloudCore has now granted your engagement team Consultant access, and it is narrow by design: the public site, three policies (privacy, risk management, policy management), the employee handbook, and one public article about the breach. Nothing else. Today you triage that material against the A.5 / A.6 / A.7 control themes and the ISMS Clauses 4–10, and you form an opinion you would defend to your audit manager.

Pacing & homework. This workshop interleaves with today's slides (briefing → activity → briefing → activity). Two hours goes fast. Anything we don't finish in class, complete as homework before the tuition-free break.

Why this matters: this is the Act I finale. Forming a defensible readiness opinion from limited evidence is exactly the judgement a certification auditor makes at a Stage 1 review. Your outputs today also feed your Field Journal entry.

The discipline of this unit is substantiate, don't assume. A preliminary opinion is only as strong as its evidence. Over-claim and you are negligent; under-claim and you are useless.

Scenario

CloudCore Networks, Perth B2B cloud infrastructure provider (own data centres: Malaga primary + Sydney DR; multi-tenant), ~250 staff, 500+ client organisations, pursuing ISO/IEC 27001 certification. You have Consultant access today, and no more. The tuition-free week ends Act I; Act II opens with Prove? (Module 7), where your engagement team receives CloudCore's evidence pack in the workshop, log extracts, change records, and interview transcripts. Your job is to leave today with a defensible, evidence-qualified readiness opinion.

Part 1, Engagement reset & evidence inventory (15 min)

Quick team introductions: name, one CloudCore artefact you have actually looked at this semester, and your single biggest "I'm not sure about this" question from Act I.

Then build an evidence inventory: list everything you have genuinely been given, the public site from Modules 1–5, plus today's three policies, employee handbook, and public breach article. Mark each item document, published claim, assertion, or third-party report. It should be a short list, that is the point.

Team question: of the four documentation adequacy tests (existence, completeness, currency, implementation), which can your current evidence actually support, and which can it not?

Part 2, ISMS documentation triage (25 min)

Judge CloudCore's management system against Clauses 4–10 and the three-tier documentation hierarchy.

For each row, state what you would expect to see, what (if anything) your evidence shows, and your adequacy rating.

Clause / document Expected (Tier) What your evidence shows Adequacy (Exist · Complete · Current · Implemented)
4–5 ISMS scope & policy (Tier 1)
5 Leadership / named security owner (A.5.2)
6 Risk assessment & treatment methodology; RTP (Tier 2/3)
6 Statement of Applicability (SoA) (Tier 3)
7 Competence, awareness, documented information
8 Operation (operationalising risk assessment & treatment)
9 Monitoring, measurement, internal audit, management review
10 Nonconformity & corrective action (incident-driven improvement)

Critical thinking: if CloudCore produced a glossy SoA listing all 93 controls but no risk treatment justification behind them, which adequacy test fails, and what is your finding?

Part 3, Control walk-through: A.5 / A.6 / A.7 (35 min)

Assess the three non-technical themes using the evidence you have. For each cluster, record the control theme, the CloudCore signal (what your evidence or the earlier modules suggest), and your preliminary verdict using the three buckets: Can assess · Qualified · Defer to Act II.

Theme cluster CloudCore signal (from your evidence) Verdict Rationale & next evidence
A.5.2 / A.5.4 Governance & leadership
A.5.3 Segregation of duties (push / approve / deploy)
A.5.15–18 Access lifecycle & least privilege
A.5.19–23 Suppliers & cloud services (responsibility split with tenants and upstream suppliers)
A.5.24–27 Incident management & NDB readiness
A.5.31 / A.5.34 Legal/regulatory & privacy (APPs)
A.6.1–6.4 Screening, terms, awareness, disciplinary
A.6.5 Offboarding (the 3–5 day window)
A.6.7 Remote working
A.7.1–7.2 Perimeter & entry (server closet, badges)
A.7.4 / A.7.5 Monitoring & environmental threats
A.7.9 / A.7.14 Off-premises assets & secure disposal

Team discussion: which two clusters are you most confident about, and which two are you most likely to defer? Why?

Part 4, Integration gap analysis (25 min)

Controls fail in chains, not in isolation. Trace each thread across A.5 / A.6 / A.7 and find the broken link.

Thread A.5 link A.6 link A.7 link Broken link? (finding)
Offboarding an engineer A.5.18 access rights revoked A.6.5 responsibilities after termination A.7.14 laptop wiped & certified
Reporting a phishing email A.5.24–27 incident plan A.6.8 event reporting channel A.7.4 monitoring context
Disposing of a retired disk A.5.9 asset inventory A.6.5 return of assets A.7.14 secure disposal
A contractor visiting the office A.5.19–20 supplier agreement A.6.6 confidentiality / NDA A.7.6 working in secure areas

Critical thinking: for one broken link, write a one-sentence finding in the form "Control X is [absent / weak / untested], which means [risk], because [evidence gap]." (This is a dry-run of the 5C+R format you will formalise in Module 11.)

Part 5, Form a preliminary readiness opinion (20 min)

Now form the opinion. As a team, agree a single preliminary readiness verdict for CloudCore's non-technical control environment, on this scale:

  • Not ready, fundamental management-system gaps (e.g. no scope, no policy, no owner).
  • Early-stage, system partially established; many controls documented but not implemented.
  • Developing, system established; most controls in place but untested or with integration gaps.
  • Approaching readiness, system and controls substantially in place; deferrals are testing, not existence.

Defend your verdict with:

  1. What you can assess (and the evidence for it).
  2. What is qualified (partially evidenced, state the caveat).
  3. What you defer to Act II (the audit programme for Modules 7–11).
  4. The single highest-priority gap you would raise with CloudCore's board first, and on what evidence.

A Stage 1 opinion is not a certification recommendation. You are assessing readiness for a Stage 2 audit, not granting certification. Hold that line.

Evaluate an AI readiness opinion (10 min). A teammate pasted this AI-generated verdict into your shared doc:

"CloudCore appears ready for its Stage 1 certification review. The ISMS scope and policy are documented, an information security owner has been named, and Annex A controls are substantially in place. With a Statement of Applicability covering all 93 controls, readiness is approaching."

As the human auditor, interrogate the opinion rather than accepting it:

  1. What evidence does the AI actually cite, and where does "documented" quietly stand in for "implemented"?
  2. What has it omitted that Clauses 6-10 (risk treatment, internal audit, management review, corrective action) and the A.6/A.7 people and physical themes would require you to see before you could agree?
  3. Where do you disagree? Rewrite the verdict in one sentence using the three-bucket discipline (Can assess · Qualified · Defer to Act II).

Deliverable

A documented Stage-1-style readiness pack: the evidence inventory (Part 1), the documentation triage (Part 2), the control walk-through with verdicts (Part 3), the integration findings (Part 4), and the team's preliminary readiness opinion with the Act II deferral list (Part 5). This pack is the spine of a credible Stage 1 readiness opinion, feeds this week's Field Journal entry, and is the working basis for Assessment 2.

Discussion

  • Why is Annex A not the substance of ISO/IEC 27001, and why does that matter for your opinion?
  • What is the difference between a control that exists and one that is implemented, and how do you tell from a document set this thin?
  • Which single deferral is the most important to name explicitly, and why?
  • How does your opinion change if CloudCore's board has never seen a security report?

The slides are a light scaffold, not the whole story. The real content is the pre-class reading; class time is for doing the audit work, and the assessment differentiates on depth. This module: pre-class (you) → 2-hour workshop (interleaved briefings + activities) → Field Journal (last 15 min).

📽️ Lecture slides{target="_blank"}: the picture-led framing deck for the workshop.

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

  1. Classify audit evidence into the four types, physical, documentary, testimonial, and analytical, and judge which is most persuasive for a given CloudCore assertion.
  2. Apply scoping and sampling methods (statistical and judgmental) to gather sufficient appropriate evidence without auditing everything.
  3. Resolve conflicting evidence by corroborating across sources, conducting targeted interviews, and documenting the rationale for every conclusion.
  4. Protect evidence integrity and chain of custody from the moment of collection through to the Evidence Locker (ISO 19011; A.5.28 Collection of evidence).

Prove?

Across the first six modules you built the case from the outside, mandates, risk, frameworks, scope, control objectives, and a readiness read of CloudCore taken with limited access. Then came the tuition-free break. Now the engagement escalates: your team is no longer working from what CloudCore publishes about itself. Your engagement team receives a synthetic training evidence pack (log extracts, IAM and directory exports, change records, and interview transcripts), modelled on CloudCore but not CloudCore's records. That shift, from what they tell us to what we can prove, is where Act II begins. The module's word, Prove?, asks the question behind every audit conclusion: what evidence would substantiate (or refute) your suspicions? The discipline is unchanged from the first module, substantiate, don't assume, but now you finally have the material to do it for real.

Component Duration Description
Pre-class reading ~45 min Self-paced reading on evidence types, sampling, collection tools, and chain of custody (pre-class/)
In-class workshop 2 hours Hands-on evidence task against CloudCore: sample, reconcile conflicting evidence, and secure the chain of custody (in-class/)
Field Journal last 15 min Handwritten reflection, handed in at the door

Before the workshop, complete:

  1. [ ] Read: pre-class/01-concepts.qmd
  2. [ ] Complete the pre-class quiz on Blackboard
  3. [ ] Re-read what CloudCore itself publishes at `` under your Consultant access, then read the synthetic evidence-pack index{target="_blank"} issued for this workshop, note what the exhibits let you test that the published documents never could.

The pack is a synthetic training set. It is modelled on CloudCore so you can practise evidence collection, sampling, and reconciliation, but it is not the client's actual evidence and must not be cited in Assessment 2 or Assessment 3. In A3 you work from the canonical CloudCore evidence released at Auditor access. The method transfers; the facts do not.

  1. [ ] AI task: Take the sample log extract{target="_blank"} from the synthetic training pack (about 30 to 40 lines modelled on CloudCore's firewall, VPN and SIEM records), paste it into an AI assistant and ask it to flag anomalies: failed logins after hours, privilege escalations, access from unusual locations, or gaps in the log. Then judge its output yourself: which flags point to real events in your sample, what did it miss, and did it invent an entry that was never there? You are the auditor here, not the AI. Save the transcript. Acknowledge the conversation as a source wherever its ideas reach your working papers, the same standard you would apply to a research paper, a vendor guide, or a colleague's suggestion. An AI conversation is part of your evidence base, never the source of truth: corroborate it like any other testimony before a finding rests on it. - CnD (Ch 12, VETF): verify, evaluate, and test the AI's evidence analysis before you accept a single flag. AI surfaces genuine anomalies, but it also misses what matters and fabricates entries that were never logged.

Concept 1: The four types of evidence

  • Physical, tangible, inspectable (server-room keypad, CCTV, cabling, hardware).
  • Documentary, written/digital records (policies, change logs, access reviews, the Statement of Applicability).
  • Testimonial, what people tell you (interviews, questionnaires, explanations).
  • Analytical, derived from data (vulnerability scans, log trends, risk-treatment comparisons). Detail lives in pre-class/01-concepts.qmd.

Concept 2: Sufficient appropriate evidence & sampling

You can never audit everything. ISO 19011 frames evidence by sufficiency (enough) and appropriateness (relevant and reliable). Statistical sampling uses maths to give confidence levels; judgmental sampling targets high-risk items from experience. Document the rationale either way.

Concept 3: Corroboration and red flags

A single source rarely proves anything. Triangulate, physical + documentary + testimonial + analytical. Watch for red flags: outdated policies, missing approvals, gaps in logs, claims of compliance without supporting records.

Concept 4: Chain of custody & evidence integrity

From the moment you collect it, evidence must stay intact, attributable, and confidential. Standardised naming, metadata, a master index, encrypted storage, and access controls protect it, and make it defensible (A.5.28 Collection of evidence).

Five-minute interactive: Evidence or Assertion?{target="_blank"} — ten artefacts: would you sign off on each? documents prove design, records prove operation. Best played before the workshop; bring your result to class.

• Find a recent practitioner blog or paper on audit sampling methodology and work out when it recommends statistical sampling versus judgemental sampling, and for which kinds of controls.
  • Search for a real audit working paper template and trace how each piece of evidence is referenced, indexed, and cross-linked back to a control and a finding.

Workshop activity: Evidence, sample, reconcile, and protect

  • Focus: classify and sample CloudCore evidence, reconcile a real conflict between policy, management's claim, and system logs, then secure what you collect.

Concept 1: The Australian privacy regime

The Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and its 13 Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) are the primary audit criteria for most Australian organisations, enforced by the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC). The APPs run from open-and-transparent management (APP 1) through collection (APP 3), use/disclosure (APP 6), cross-border disclosure (APP 8), and security (APP 11) to access and correction (APP 12–13). The NDB scheme requires notification to the OAIC and affected individuals when a breach is likely to result in serious harm.

Concept 2: The data lifecycle, classify, mask, delete

ISO/IEC 27001:2022 added three cloud-era controls central to privacy: A.8.10 Information deletion, A.8.11 Data masking, and A.8.12 Data leakage prevention. Combined with A.5.12 Classification and A.5.34 Privacy and protection of PII, they cover the whole lifecycle, protect what you have, hide it where you don't need to see it, and remove it when you no longer need it.

Concept 3: Cross-border and third-party processing

APP 8 governs disclosure of personal information overseas. For CloudCore, with data in its own Australian data centres but potential US-based analytics, the auditor tests whether transfer mechanisms (contracts, binding obligations, adequacy) provide substantially similar protection, and whether the PIA for any cross-border processing actually exists.

Concept 4: Technical safeguards, access & encryption

The technical backbone of APP 11: role-based access control (RBAC) aligned to least privilege, multi-factor authentication for sensitive access, encryption at rest and in transit, and tested key management. The auditor does not take the policy at face value, they test the configuration.

Concept 5: Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs)

A PIA is a systematic process for identifying and mitigating privacy risks before a new processing activity goes live. The auditor assesses both the process (are PIAs triggered at the right time?) and the quality (are risks actually mitigated, with monitoring?).

Five-minute interactive: Data Border Crossing{target="_blank"}: eight privacy scenarios (GDPR reach, APP 8, NDB and erasure) mapped onto CloudCore's data flows. Best played before the workshop; bring your result to class.

• Find the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner's latest Notifiable Data Breaches statistics report and identify which sectors report the most breaches, the leading causes, and how those trends have shifted over recent reporting periods.
  • Locate a current Privacy Impact Assessment template published by an Australian government agency or a reputable consultancy, and compare its structure and risk-rating approach to the mini-PIA you completed in the workshop.

This module's anchor controls are A.5.34 Privacy and protection of PII (the ISO hook for the APPs) and the lifecycle controls A.8.10 Information deletion and A.8.11 Data masking, supported by A.5.12 Classification, A.8.12 Data leakage prevention, A.8.33 Test information, and the regulatory hook A.5.31 Legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements (which captures the Privacy Act). The Australian overlay is the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), the 13 APPs, and the NDB scheme. See the derived ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Control Reference. Paraphrase, never reproduce verbatim ISO text.

You are a junior auditor on the CloudCore engagement. In the previous module (Comply?) you stress-tested the policies. In this module you turn to the asset those policies exist to defend: CloudCore's customer and tenant data, the crown jewel. Today's scenarios are hands-on learning exercises that build the privacy-audit mindset; your deliverables feed this week's Field Journal.

Scenario

CloudCore Networks, Perth B2B cloud infrastructure provider (own data centres: Malaga primary + Sydney DR; multi-tenant), ~250 staff, 500+ client organisations, pursuing ISO/IEC 27001 certification. Your engagement team receives a data-protection evidence pack today, supplied in the workshop as static exhibits: the canonical privacy policy, POL-DATA-023{target="_blank"}, a data-inventory extract{target="_blank"}, the access-review register{target="_blank"} (reissued from Module 7), and the PIA register{target="_blank"}. (The live case-study platform stays at Consultant access; these documents come to you as handouts, not as a login.) Your audit team will map CloudCore's PII, run a serious-harm assessment on a breach, and complete a mini-PIA before this week's Field Journal.
Mixed pack: canonical policy plus synthetic exhibits

The privacy policy is CloudCore's canonical policy. The data-inventory extract, access-review register and PIA register are synthetic workshop exhibits, built to give you realistic material to test. They are not client records and must not be cited in A2 or A3. In A3 you apply the same method to the canonical Auditor-access records.

Carry the discipline of this unit into every task: substantiate, don't assume. A policy that says "we minimise" is a claim; your job is to test it against the evidence.

• Privacy Act 1988 (Cth): the main Australian law on handling personal information.
  • APPs (Australian Privacy Principles): the 13 rules in the Privacy Act, for example APP 6 (use and disclosure), APP 8 (sending data overseas) and APP 11 (security).
  • OAIC (Office of the Australian Information Commissioner): the regulator that enforces the Privacy Act.
  • NDB scheme (Notifiable Data Breaches): the part of the Privacy Act that covers data breaches. If personal information is accessed, disclosed or lost without authorisation, and this is likely to cause serious harm to any individual, it is an eligible data breach. The organisation must then notify the OAIC and the affected individuals. Part 3 walks you through the test.
  • Serious harm: judged for each individual, taking into account how sensitive the data is, how likely it is to be misused, and what has been done to reduce the risk. It is not a count of records.
  • PII (personally identifiable information): the ISO term for personal information.
  • PIA (Privacy Impact Assessment): a structured review of the privacy risks of a new project, done before it goes live.

The NDB timing rules (when the clock starts, and what the 30 days are for) are in the pre-class reading, section 2. Working them out is part of Part 3.

Part 1, Locate the crown jewel (15 min)

Quick team introductions: name, one app or service you use that holds personal information about you, and your biggest concern about how it's protected.

Then, as a team, brainstorm the personal information CloudCore holds. A B2B cloud infrastructure provider doesn't just hold its own staff data, it holds, on behalf of each enterprise customer:

  • Customer-organisation data, company name, billing, contract terms, named account administrators.
  • End-user data, for each customer's own users (employees, students, patients depending on the tenant): names, emails, usage logs, sometimes uploaded content.
  • Staff data, HR records, access credentials, performance data.
  • Third-party data, analytics vendors, sub-processors, support tooling.

Your task: build a one-page personal-information inventory with at least eight data categories, the system each lives in, and a sensitivity rating (Restricted / Confidential / Internal / Public).

Part 2, Classify, mask, delete (25 min)

For each high-sensitivity category in your inventory, judge CloudCore's lifecycle controls:

Data category Classification (A.5.12) Masking in non-prod? (A.8.11) Retention schedule + secure deletion? (A.8.10) DLP / egress monitoring? (A.8.12)

Team discussion: Which single category is the most poorly defended across the lifecycle, and which ISO/IEC 27001:2022 control would you raise first?

Part 3, NDB serious-harm assessment (30 min)

CloudCore's SOC flags an incident: a misconfigured object-storage bucket on CloudCore's own tenant storage platform exposed a tenant's exported customer list (names, work emails, job titles, and, because the customer opted to store it, a custom field containing partial Medicare numbers for 4,200 of their staff) for 11 days before it was secured. The bucket logs show three unauthorised IP addresses accessed the object.

Apply the NDB three-question test:

  1. Unauthorised access, disclosure, or loss?, Document what the evidence shows.
  2. Likely to result in serious harm?, Assess per-individual. Consider data sensitivity (identity documents, contact data), likelihood of misuse (was the data encrypted at rest? were copies taken?), and mitigations.
  3. Reasonable steps to prevent serious harm?, Are there steps that would still reduce the risk?

Decide as a team:

  • Is this an eligible data breach? (Y/N, with reasoning.)
  • What is the 30-day OAIC assessment window, and when is notification due? (Which clock starts from when?)
  • Which individuals must be notified, and how would you word the harm they face?

Critical thinking: How does your assessment change if the partial Medicare numbers were not in the custom field? Why is "serious harm" not a headcount?

Part 4, Mini-PIA for CloudCore's new AI feature (30 min)

CloudCore is about to launch "CloudCore Insights", an AI feature that analyses tenant usage patterns to recommend workflow improvements. Training data is processed in a US-East cloud region operated by a US-based sub-processor. No PIA has been done.

Complete a mini-PIA in your team:

  1. Trigger, is this the kind of processing that requires a PIA? Why?
  2. Data flow, what personal information flows where? Map collection → processing → storage → cross-border transfer → retention/deletion.
  3. Privacy risks, identify the top five, mapped to APPs (e.g. APP 6 secondary use; APP 8 cross-border; APP 11 security; APP 10 data quality / model bias).
  4. Mitigations, for each risk, propose a control (technical, organisational, or legal), and say whether it is implemented, planned, or missing.
  5. Ongoing monitoring, what would you reassess, and when?

Cross-border focus: What transfer mechanism would make the US processing substantially similar in protection? What would you require in the sub-processor contract?

Part 5, Defending the crown jewel (20 min)

Drawing on Parts 2–4, agree your team's top three prioritised findings for CloudCore's board. For each:

  • The control gap (which ISO/IEC 27001:2022 control or APP).
  • The evidence you'd cite (technical testing, documentation, interview).
  • The risk if unfixed.
  • The recommended fix and a realistic timeframe.

Rank them by risk to the crown jewel, not by ease of fix.

Evaluate the AI (5 min). Before you sign off, a teammate pastes this AI-generated PIA summary for CloudCore Insights into the workpapers and asks whether it clears the feature to launch:

AI output: "Privacy Impact Assessment, CloudCore Insights. The feature analyses tenant usage patterns to recommend workflow improvements. Recommendation: encrypt all data at rest and in transit with AES-256. With encryption applied across the environment, privacy risks are mitigated and residual risk is low. The feature is safe to launch. No further controls required."

You are the auditor, not the AI. "Encrypt everything" is a security blanket, not a PIA, and encryption does not address most privacy obligations. Identify what the AI oversimplified:

  1. The lifecycle it skipped. Name the four dimensions this PIA never touches: data classification (A.5.12), masking of training data (A.8.11), retention and secure deletion (A.8.10), and cross-border transfer (APP 8). For each, say what encryption leaves entirely unaddressed.
  2. The cross-border blind spot. Part 4 sent tenant data to a US-East cloud region handled by a US sub-processor, yet the PIA never mentions APP 8 or a transfer mechanism. What would a human auditor require (contractual, legal, or technical) before clearing this feature, and why is encryption irrelevant to that question?
  3. The unsupported verdict. The AI rated residual risk "low" with no reasoning. Which APPs (try APP 6 secondary use, APP 10 data quality and model bias, APP 11 security) did it fail to assess, and what would push the rating the other way?

Provenance. This PIA is now sitting in the workpapers with nothing on it to say an AI wrote it, no author, no date, no note of what it was given to assess. A Privacy Impact Assessment is a document an organisation may have to stand behind to the OAIC; if the regulator asked who assessed the residual risk as "low", your file has no answer. An auditor who cannot say where a working paper came from has a defective working paper, whatever the source was. Add the attribution line this PIA needs, author or tool, date, inputs assessed, reviewer, and apply the same rule to your own AI-assisted entries.

Group output: rewrite the AI's one-line verdict naming at least two privacy risks that encryption does not solve.

Then reflect: which finding surprised you most, and which control, if it held, would do most to protect CloudCore's customer data?

Deliverable

A completed PII inventory + classification table, a documented NDB serious-harm assessment with a clear eligible/not-eligible decision and notification timeline, a completed mini-PIA with mapped risks and mitigations, and a prioritised top-three findings list with evidence and fixes. These feed your Field Journal entry this week.

Discussion

  • Why is "serious harm" assessed per-individual rather than by record count, and how does that change the auditor's job?
  • How does professional skepticism apply to a claim like "we minimise data collection"?
  • If you could fix only one data-protection control at CloudCore before certification, which would it be, and on what evidence?

The slides are a light scaffold, not the whole story. The real content is the pre-class reading; class time is for doing the audit work, not re-reading slides at you. The further you pull (pre-class + self-study), the deeper your learning; the assessment differentiates on depth. In each module: pre-class (you) → 2-hour workshop (interleaved briefings + activities) → Field Journal (last 15 min).
